results.name: prime_set_prime_target_lift
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all prime, yes rate for non-example prime targets minus non-example odd composite targets; observed above null means people generalise along primality more sharply than the model, below means less.
results.code:
# name: prime_set_prime_target_lift
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all prime, yes rate for non-example prime targets minus non-example odd composite targets; observed above null means people generalise along primality more sharply than the model, below means less.
def _ex(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = (~np.isnan(E)).sum(1)
    isex = (E == t[:, None]).any(1)
    return E, t, r, n, isex

def _rate(r, m):
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    E, t, r, n, isex = _ex(df)
    P = np.array([k > 1 and all(k % d for d in range(2, int(k ** 0.5) + 1)) for k in range(0, 101)])
    Ei = np.nan_to_num(E, nan=0).astype(int).clip(0, 100)
    allp = (P[Ei] | np.isnan(E)).all(1) & (n >= 2)
    tp = P[t.astype(int).clip(0, 100)]
    oddc = (t % 2 == 1) & ~tp & (t > 1)
    return _rate(r, allp & ~isex & tp) - _rate(r, allp & ~isex & oddc)

results.name: round_decade_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets that are multiples of 10, on sets containing no multiple of 10, minus the yes rate for other non-example targets on those sets; observed above null means round numbers are spuriously salient as yes answers beyond the model's rules, below means they are avoided.
results.code:
# name: round_decade_target_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets that are multiples of 10, on sets containing no multiple of 10, minus the yes rate for other non-example targets on those sets; observed above null means round numbers are spuriously salient as yes answers beyond the model's rules, below means they are avoided.
def _ex(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = (~np.isnan(E)).sum(1)
    isex = (E == t[:, None]).any(1)
    return E, t, r, n, isex

def _rate(r, m):
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    E, t, r, n, isex = _ex(df)
    no10 = ~((E % 10 == 0).any(1))
    m = no10 & ~isex
    rd = t % 10 == 0
    return _rate(r, m & rd) - _rate(r, m & ~rd)

results.name: above_max_minus_below_min
results.description: Among non-example targets outside the example range by 1-15, yes rate for targets above the largest example minus targets below the smallest; observed above null means people extend generalisation upward more than downward (asymmetry the symmetric interval model lacks), below means the reverse.
results.code:
# name: above_max_minus_below_min
# description: Among non-example targets outside the example range by 1-15, yes rate for targets above the largest example minus targets below the smallest; observed above null means people extend generalisation upward more than downward (asymmetry the symmetric interval model lacks), below means the reverse.
def _ex(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = (~np.isnan(E)).sum(1)
    isex = (E == t[:, None]).any(1)
    return E, t, r, n, isex

def _rate(r, m):
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    E, t, r, n, isex = _ex(df)
    mx = np.nanmax(E, 1); mn = np.nanmin(E, 1)
    up = (t > mx) & (t - mx <= 15)
    dn = (t < mn) & (mn - t <= 15)
    return _rate(r, up & ~isex) - _rate(r, dn & ~isex)

results.name: power2_set_power2_target_lift
results.description: On sets of 2+ examples that are all powers of 2, yes rate for non-example power-of-2 targets minus non-example even targets that are not powers of 2; observed above null means people commit to powers-of-2 more than the model (exponent cost too high), below means less.
results.code:
# name: power2_set_power2_target_lift
# description: On sets of 2+ examples that are all powers of 2, yes rate for non-example power-of-2 targets minus non-example even targets that are not powers of 2; observed above null means people commit to powers-of-2 more than the model (exponent cost too high), below means less.
def _ex(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = (~np.isnan(E)).sum(1)
    isex = (E == t[:, None]).any(1)
    return E, t, r, n, isex

def _rate(r, m):
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    E, t, r, n, isex = _ex(df)
    p2 = np.isin(np.arange(101), [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64])
    Ei = np.nan_to_num(E, nan=0).astype(int).clip(0, 100)
    allp = (p2[Ei] | np.isnan(E)).all(1) & (n >= 2)
    tp = p2[t.astype(int).clip(0, 100)]
    return _rate(r, allp & ~isex & tp) - _rate(r, allp & ~isex & ~tp & (t % 2 == 0))

results.name: shared_digit_nonending_target_yes
results.description: On sets of 2+ examples that all contain some common digit d, yes rate for non-example targets that contain d but do not end in d, minus the yes rate for non-example targets lacking d; observed above null means people use a contains-digit rule more than the model, below means less.
results.code:
# name: shared_digit_nonending_target_yes
# description: On sets of 2+ examples that all contain some common digit d, yes rate for non-example targets that contain d but do not end in d, minus the yes rate for non-example targets lacking d; observed above null means people use a contains-digit rule more than the model, below means less.
def _ex(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = (~np.isnan(E)).sum(1)
    isex = (E == t[:, None]).any(1)
    return E, t, r, n, isex

def _rate(r, m):
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    E, t, r, n, isex = _ex(df)
    Ei = np.nan_to_num(E, nan=-1).astype(int)
    ti = t.astype(int)
    lift_m1 = np.zeros(len(t), bool); lift_m0 = np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    for d in range(10):
        def has(x):
            return ((x % 10) == d) | (((x // 10) % 10 == d) & (x >= 10)) | ((x == 100) & (d in (0, 1)))
        allc = (has(Ei) | (Ei < 0)).all(1) & (n >= 2)
        lift_m1 |= allc & has(ti) & (ti % 10 != d)
        lift_m0 |= allc & ~has(ti)
    lift_m0 &= ~lift_m1
    return _rate(r, lift_m1 & ~isex) - _rate(r, lift_m0 & ~isex)

results.name: same_row_vs_adjacent_row_near
results.description: Among non-example targets 1-5 away from the nearest example, yes rate when the target is in the same hundred-chart row (1-10, 11-20, ...) as that nearest example minus when it is in a different row; observed above null means chart-row boundaries matter more than the model's row-range bonus implies, below means less.
results.code:
# name: same_row_vs_adjacent_row_near
# description: Among non-example targets 1-5 away from the nearest example, yes rate when the target is in the same hundred-chart row (1-10, 11-20, ...) as that nearest example minus when it is in a different row; observed above null means chart-row boundaries matter more than the model's row-range bonus implies, below means less.
def _ex(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = (~np.isnan(E)).sum(1)
    isex = (E == t[:, None]).any(1)
    return E, t, r, n, isex

def _rate(r, m):
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    E, t, r, n, isex = _ex(df)
    dist = np.abs(E - t[:, None])
    dmin = np.nanmin(dist, 1)
    j = np.nanargmin(np.where(np.isnan(dist), 1e9, dist), 1)
    near = E[np.arange(len(t)), j]
    row = lambda x: np.floor((x - 1) / 10)
    m = ~isex & (dmin >= 1) & (dmin <= 5)
    same = row(near) == row(t)
    return _rate(r, m & same) - _rate(r, m & ~same)

results.name: setsize_nonexample_yes_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes (0/1) on number of examples (1-4) among non-example targets; observed more negative than null means people narrow their generalisation with more examples faster than the size principle predicts, less negative/positive means slower.
results.code:
# name: setsize_nonexample_yes_slope
# description: OLS slope of yes (0/1) on number of examples (1-4) among non-example targets; observed more negative than null means people narrow their generalisation with more examples faster than the size principle predicts, less negative/positive means slower.
def _ex(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = (~np.isnan(E)).sum(1)
    isex = (E == t[:, None]).any(1)
    return E, t, r, n, isex

def _rate(r, m):
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    E, t, r, n, isex = _ex(df)
    m = ~isex
    x = n[m].astype(float); y = r[m]
    xc = x - x.mean()
    return float((xc * (y - y.mean())).sum() / max((xc ** 2).sum(), 1e-9))

results.name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples, among non-example targets within 10 of some example, yes rate for targets strictly closer to the last-shown example than the first minus those strictly closer to the first; observed above null means a recency effect in generalisation (model is order-invariant), below means a primacy effect.
results.code:
# name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
# description: For sets of 2+ examples, among non-example targets within 10 of some example, yes rate for targets strictly closer to the last-shown example than the first minus those strictly closer to the first; observed above null means a recency effect in generalisation (model is order-invariant), below means a primacy effect.
def _ex(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = (~np.isnan(E)).sum(1)
    isex = (E == t[:, None]).any(1)
    return E, t, r, n, isex

def _rate(r, m):
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    E, t, r, n, isex = _ex(df)
    first = E[:, 0]
    idx = np.clip(n - 1, 0, E.shape[1] - 1)
    last = E[np.arange(len(t)), idx]
    df_ = np.abs(t - first); dl = np.abs(t - last)
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), 1)
    m = (n >= 2) & ~isex & (dmin <= 10)
    return _rate(r, m & (dl < df_)) - _rate(r, m & (df_ < dl))
